commands.what: Every account with its status, failed-attempt count and group memberships.
One account in full, as the directory sees it.

commands.command: python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> --actor helpdesk --reason 'user verified by phone' unlock aisha.khan
commands.what: Unlock an account and reset its failed attempts, recording who asked and why.
Lock an account without deleting it — a security hold while an incident is investigated.
Disable an account for good (leaver, contractor expiry). Disabled is a status, not a lock.
Add a group membership. Nothing else about the account changes.
Remove the membership that is no longer needed — least privilege is a removal, not a promise.
Live sessions with the device they were issued to.

commands.command: python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> revoke-session aisha.khan-laptop --reason 'device not seen for 30 days'
commands.what: Kill one session by id. This is the step students most often forget.
The last 20 changes with actor, action, target and reason — your evidence.
The same data over HTTP, if the service is running. This is what a real integration would call.

exercises.prompt: Aisha Khan is locked out after failed attempts and has telephoned the service desk. Unlock her account and show the audit entry that proves the change.
exercises.solution:
python3 lib/idp.py --state /var/lib/ontrak-idp/directory.json \
  --actor helpdesk --reason "caller verified: aisha.khan, staff id 4711" unlock aisha.khan
python3 lib/idp.py --state /var/lib/ontrak-idp/directory.json audit

exercises.prompt: Marco Silva moves to finance. He needs finance and must keep finance-reporting, but must lose warehouse.
exercises.solution:
python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> add-member marco.silva finance
python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> remove-member marco.silva warehouse

exercises.prompt: A contractor's agreement ended last month and their account is still active in two groups. Close it down and record why.
exercises.solution:
python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> disable c.nguyen --reason "contract ended 2026-08-31"
python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> list-sessions

exercises.prompt: A laptop that has not been seen for a month still holds an active session for Aisha Khan. End it.
exercises.solution:
python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> list-sessions
python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> revoke-session <session-id> --reason "device not seen for 30 days"

objectives: Read an account's status, groups and failed attempts from the directory
Unlock, disable and re-enable accounts, and understand when each is right
Add and remove group membership without accidentally widening access
Revoke a live session and record the reason

steps.body: A locked account keeps every group membership it had; it just cannot authenticate. A disabled account is out of service entirely. An account whose memberships are wrong is a third, separate problem — and the three have three different fixes. Read the account before you change anything: the wrong fix here either leaves the user unable to work or leaves access open.
steps.title: Status is not the same as membership

steps.body: Lockouts from failed attempts are routine and are undone with an unlock, which also clears the counter. Disabling is a deliberate removal of access (a leaver, an expired contract) and should never be used to fix a typo'd password.
steps.command: python3 lib/idp.py --state <file> unlock aisha.khan --reason 'verified by phone'
steps.title: Unlocking is a fix; disabling is a decision

steps.body: When somebody moves team, the new membership is the visible half of the ticket. The other half is that their old access goes away — otherwise access only ever grows, and the audit becomes worthless. Name both in the same change.
steps.title: Least privilege means removing the old one

steps.body: Changing a status or a password does not necessarily end a session that is already open — a laptop that signed in last week stays signed in. If the ticket says the device is gone, revoking the session is part of the job.
steps.title: Sessions outlive password changes

steps.body: Every command above records an actor, an action, a target and a reason. Use --reason for anything that grants or removes access: it is the difference between "someone changed it" and a change you can defend a month later.
steps.title: The audit trail is the deliverable

identity-directory-admin.yaml.summary: Work the three identity tickets a service desk gets every week — an account locked out, somebody moving team, and a session that should no longer be alive — against a directory service, leaving an audit trail that shows what you did and why.
identity-directory-admin.yaml.title: Account administration: locks, groups and sessions

commands.what: Print the directory you are currently in.
List everything, including dotfiles, with permissions, owner, size and date.
Create directories, and their parents, in one step. Brace expansion builds the whole tree.
Create an empty file, or update the timestamp of an existing one.
Copy, preserving permissions, ownership and timestamps (the "right" way for a tree).

commands.danger: mv silently replaces the destination. Use `mv -n` to refuse instead.
commands.what: Rename, or move to another directory. Silent overwrite if the target exists.

commands.danger: There is no recycle bin. `rm -rf /` is unrecoverable — check your path with pwd first.
commands.what: Delete a directory and everything inside it.
Find files by name, owner, permissions or age. Far faster than guessing.
Ask what a file actually is, rather than trusting its extension.
See what is eating disk space, largest last.

exercises.prompt: Create /srv/projects/bravo with src, tests and docs subdirectories, and an empty README.md at the top of it.
exercises.solution:
mkdir -p /srv/projects/bravo/{src,tests,docs}
touch /srv/projects/bravo/README.md

exercises.prompt: Something is filling /var/log with files named *.old. Find them and delete only those.
exercises.solution:
find /var/log -type f -name '*.old' -print
find /var/log -type f -name '*.old' -delete

objectives: Create and remove directories, including parents in one step
Inspect file contents and metadata without an editor
Find a file by name, owner or age

steps.body: Linux has no drive letters. One tree starts at /, and every file lives somewhere in it. /srv is conventionally where a site puts services, /etc is configuration, /var is changing data such as logs, and /tmp is disposable. When a ticket says "the app cannot write its uploads", the question is always *which path* and *who owns it*.
steps.title: Everything is a path

steps.body: Before creating or deleting anything under a path, confirm what is already there and who owns it. `ls -la` answers all of that in one line, and reading it is a habit that prevents most self-inflicted outages.
steps.title: Look before you write

steps.body: Brace expansion plus -p means a whole project skeleton in a single step, and it is idempotent: running it again changes nothing.
steps.title: Create the tree in one command

steps.body: In a real incident you are rarely handed the path. `find` with -name, -user or -mtime is how you locate "the log that was written yesterday" without walking the tree by hand.
steps.title: Find it again

linux-files-and-dirs.yaml.summary: Create, inspect, move and delete files and directories from the shell, and find them again afterwards — the four commands every other Linux ticket depends on.
linux-files-and-dirs.yaml.title: Files, directories and finding things

commands.what: Third and fourth columns are the owner and the group.
Set owner and group together. Prefix with -R to recurse.
Change only the group, leaving the owner alone.

commands.danger: Without -h as root, chown follows the link and changes the target.
commands.what: Change a symlink itself rather than what it points at.
Only change the entries still owned by root, so a repair is repeatable.
List everything under a path that is not owned by the expected account — the audit query.
Show ownership and permissions for every component of a path.

exercises.prompt: /srv/www/site, and everything below it, is owned by root. The web service runs as www-data and must own the whole tree.
exercises.solution: chown -R www-data:www-data /srv/www/site

exercises.prompt: The developers group needs read and write access to /srv/projects/alpha, and nobody else should have any. Keep the owner as-is.
exercises.solution:
chgrp -R developers /srv/projects/alpha
chmod -R g+rwX,o-rwx /srv/projects/alpha

exercises.prompt: /srv/www/current is a symlink to /srv/www/releases/v3 and must be owned by www-data without touching the release.
exercises.solution: chown -h www-data /srv/www/current

objectives: Read owner and group and explain which bits they select
Change ownership of a file, a tree and a symlink correctly
Recognise when the right fix is a group, not a wider permission

steps.body: A mode of 640 means: owner rw, group r, everyone else nothing. *Which* triples you get depends on who you are and which group you are in — so the same file can be writable for one engineer and read-only for another. Ownership is how you give a service access without opening the file to the world.
steps.title: Ownership selects which bits apply

steps.body: A daemon runs as the account named in its unit file, very often www-data or nginx. If the upload directory is owned by root, the daemon cannot create files there — and the log will say "permission denied", not "wrong owner". Check with `ps -o user= -p $(pgrep -f nginx | head -1)`.
steps.title: Services run as their own user

steps.body: When three engineers need write access, adding them to a shared group and setting g+w on the directory is the fix. Widening to 777 is not: it grants the same access to every process on the machine.
steps.title: The right repair is usually a group

steps.body: -R applies the change to every entry below the path. Do it knowingly: a recursive chown on / will make the machine unbootable, and there is no undo.
steps.danger: chown -R on the wrong path (especially /) can leave a host unbootable.
steps.title: Recursion, but deliberately

linux-ownership.yaml.summary: Who a file belongs to decides which permission bits apply to you. Change ownership safely, including recursively, and diagnose the "the app runs but cannot write its own directory" class of ticket.
linux-ownership.yaml.title: Ownership with chown and chgrp

commands.what: Show the mode, owner and group. First column is type + 9 permission bits.
Print the mode in octal plus owner and group — the form you can compare in a script.
Set the mode by octal. 6=rw for the owner, 4=r for the group, 0=nothing for everyone else.
Add the execute bit for the owner only, leaving every other bit alone.
Recurse. Capital X adds execute only to directories (and to files that already had it).
Traversable and readable by the owner and the group, closed to everyone else.
Show the bits stripped from newly created files and directories.
Print the permissions of *every* directory on the path. Diagnoses "permission denied" that has nothing to do with the file itself.

exercises.prompt: /srv/app/deploy.sh must be runnable by its owner and by members of its group, but not by anyone else. Nothing else about the file should change.
exercises.solution: chmod 750 /srv/app/deploy.sh

exercises.prompt: A payroll export at /srv/app/payroll-export.csv is world-readable. Lock it down.
exercises.solution: chmod 600 /srv/app/payroll-export.csv

exercises.prompt: A service running as its own user cannot read /srv/app/config, and the files inside are already world-readable. What is wrong, and what do you change?
exercises.solution:
# The directory itself is not traversable:
namei -l /srv/app/config
chmod 755 /srv/app/config

objectives: Read the 10-character permission string and the octal equivalent
Set a file private, shared or executable on purpose
Understand why a directory needs the execute bit to be usable

steps.body: `-rwxr-x---` is: type (one character), then owner, group, other — each three bits of read (4), write (2) and execute (1). rwxr-x--- is 7, 5, 0, so the octal form is 750. Reading it the other way round is the single most common reason a "fixed" permission is still wrong.
steps.title: Read the mode as three triples

steps.body: A .sh file that is not +x cannot be run, no matter what it is called. The usual cause of "the deployment script broke overnight" is a copy or an extraction that dropped the bit.
steps.title: Executable is a permission, not a name

steps.body: Data about people — payroll, exports, keys — belongs at 600 or 640. The question is never "can I read it", it is "who else can". `find / -perm -o+r` finds the readable-by-the-world cases in an audit.
steps.title: Private means nobody else

steps.body: On a directory, r lists names and x lets you traverse into it. That is why a 750 directory is usable and a 640 directory is not, even though both look restrictive. `namei -l` shows the whole path at once.
steps.title: Directories need execute to be entered

steps.body: 777 removes the question instead of answering it, and later looks like a security finding. Decide who needs access — owner, group, or other — and grant exactly that.
steps.danger: chmod -R 777 hides the real failure and is a finding in any audit.
steps.title: Do not fix a permission error with 777

linux-permissions.yaml.summary: Read a permission string, turn it into octal, and set it correctly with chmod — including the executable, private-file and directory-crawl cases that cause most service failures.
linux-permissions.yaml.title: File permissions with chmod

commands.what: List the current user's allowed commands. The fastest way to answer "can they sudo?".
Check another user's policy. Works without being that user.
Non-interactive check — succeeds only if the command would not prompt for a password.

commands.danger: Editing sudoers with a normal editor and a typo locks everyone out of sudo.
commands.what: Edit a drop-in file with a syntax check. Always edit through visudo.
Validate every sudoers file on the box and report the first error.
One command, one group, no password. This is the shape of a real delegation.
Drop-in files must be 0440 and owned by root, or sudo ignores them.
Read every delegation currently in force.

exercises.prompt: The ops group must be able to restart nginx without a password, and nothing else. Implement it as a drop-in file and show the resulting policy.
exercises.solution:
printf '%s\n' 'ops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart nginx' > /etc/sudoers.d/ops
chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/ops
visudo -c
sudo -l -U ops

exercises.prompt: A colleague proposed `/etc/sudoers.d/helpdesk` containing `helpdesk ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL`. Explain in one line why a training lab rejects it, and write the narrow alternative for resetting one user's password.
exercises.solution:
# It grants full root with no password to everyone in the group, so a single
# compromised helpdesk account owns the estate.
printf '%s\n' 'helpdesk ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/passwd [a-z]*' > /etc/sudoers.d/helpdesk

exercises.prompt: sudo now prints "syntax error" and nobody can escalate. You still have a root shell on another tty. Recover the machine.
exercises.solution:
# visudo refuses to save a broken file, so recover by naming the bad file:
visudo -c
rm /etc/sudoers.d/<the-broken-file>
visudo -c

objectives: Explain the difference between su and sudo, and why sudo is auditable
Delegate one command to one group with a drop-in file
Validate sudoers syntax before it takes effect

steps.body: `su -` gives you a root shell and an audit trail that says "someone became root". `sudo <command>` gives one command the privilege it needs and logs which command, as whom, on which host. For a support team, the second is what you want: it is least privilege *and* the evidence you need afterwards.
steps.title: sudo is privilege per command, su is privilege for a session

steps.body: `ops ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` is indistinguishable from giving out the root password, except that nobody remembers they did it. Delegate the specific commands an operational role actually runs, and keep /etc/sudoers for the distribution's own defaults.
steps.danger: A blanket NOPASSWD:ALL rule is the finding auditors look for first.
steps.title: Never hand out a blanket rule

steps.body: /etc/sudoers.d/<name> keeps delegations reviewable and removable: delete the file and the privilege is gone. The filename must not contain a dot or end in ~, and the file must be mode 0440 owned by root, or sudo silently skips it.
steps.command:
printf '%s
' 'ops ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart nginx' > /etc/sudoers.d/ops && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/ops
steps.title: Drop-in files, one per delegation

steps.body: `visudo -c` parses the whole policy and names the first broken file. This is the single most valuable habit in this lesson: a syntax error in sudoers can take away your own root access, and if you are already root over SSH you cannot fix it from the console.
steps.title: Validate before you walk away

steps.body: A delegation is only finished when you have confirmed both halves: the intended user can run the intended command without a password, and the same user cannot run anything else.
steps.title: Prove it works, and that it does not over-grant

linux-sudo.yaml.summary: Grant a user or group exactly the privilege they need — and no more — through /etc/sudoers.d, verify it with sudo -l, and repair sudoers without locking everybody out of the machine.
linux-sudo.yaml.title: Delegating privilege with sudo

commands.what: Show a user's uid, primary group and every group they are in.
Create the account with a home directory, a login shell, and group membership.
Set or reset a password interactively. Use `chpasswd` for non-interactive scripts.
Lock the account (the hash is prefixed with !) without deleting it.

commands.danger: usermod -G without -a silently removes every other group membership.
commands.what: Add to a supplementary group. Without -a, -G *replaces* the whole list.
Create a group before adding anyone to it.

commands.danger: -r deletes files. Confirm the account is the leaver's before running it.
commands.what: Delete the account and its home directory and mail spool.
List every account and uid from the system database.
Show who has actually logged in — the fastest way to spot stale accounts.
Show password and account expiry dates.

exercises.prompt: Aisha Khan joins the support team. Create her account with a home directory and a bash shell, in the supplementary group support (creating the group if needed), and give it a password.
exercises.solution:
groupadd -f support
useradd -m -s /bin/bash -c 'Aisha Khan' -G support aisha.khan
echo 'aisha.khan:ChangeMe!23' | chpasswd

exercises.prompt: Aisha also needs the developers group. Add it without losing the support group.
exercises.solution: usermod -aG developers aisha.khan

exercises.prompt: Tom Reeves has left. Remove his account completely, including his home directory, and show that nothing is left behind.
exercises.solution:
userdel -r tom.reeves
find /home -maxdepth 1 -name 'tom.reeves' -print
find / -xdev -nouser 2>/dev/null | head

exercises.prompt: Find every account that has never logged in, excluding system accounts below uid 1000.
exercises.solution:
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd | while read -r u; do
  lastlog -u "$u" | tail -n1 | grep -q 'Never' && echo "$u"
done

objectives: Create a user with a home directory, shell and supplementary group
Reset and lock a password, and understand where the hash lives
Remove a leaver completely, including their home directory

steps.body: /etc/passwd holds the public record — name, uid, gid, home, shell — and is readable by everyone. /etc/shadow holds the password hash and is readable only by root. When a ticket says "the user says their password is wrong", the answer is in the second file: `passwd -S` prints the state without exposing the hash.
steps.title: Two files, two halves of the story

steps.body: A new starter needs an account, a group, and access. Create the group first if it does not exist, then the user with -m so the home directory and skel files appear, then set a password. Everything above is one line in an onboarding script, and running it twice should be harmless.
steps.title: Joiner

steps.body: Moving teams changes group membership, not the account. -a is mandatory: `usermod -G` replaces the list, which is how people quietly lose access they still need.
steps.title: Mover

steps.body: Offboarding is a removal, not a lock, once the person has left: a locked account still owns files and still appears in audits. Delete the account with -r, then check for leftovers with `find / -nouser` — files owned by a uid that no longer exists.
steps.title: Leaver

steps.body: "I removed the user" is a claim. The evidence is: id fails, the home directory is gone, and no files reference the old uid.
steps.title: Prove it

linux-users-and-groups.yaml.summary: Create and remove accounts and groups, set and lock passwords, and run the joiner/mover/leaver tasks a support desk gets weekly — including removing the home directory and checking nothing was left behind.
linux-users-and-groups.yaml.title: Local users and groups — joiners, movers, leavers

commands.what: Every NIC and whether it is Up. Physical up + no address is a different fault from "adapters missing".
The full picture — address, DHCP, DNS servers, gateway — in one command every technician recognises.
The same information as objects, so you can pipe it to Where-Object.
Ping plus route plus interface selection in one object. Substitute for a bare ping.
Test the DNS resolver itself, bypassing the hosts file and NetBIOS.
Prove the service is reachable by name, not just that the name resolves.
Which resolvers each adapter is actually using.
Drop the client cache after any resolver change, so the next test tells the truth.
Check for a manual override that makes a name resolve even when DNS is broken.

exercises.prompt: A laptop shows "no internet". It has address 169.254.43.7 and no gateway. Say what the fault is and what you check next.
exercises.solution:
# 169.254.x.x is APIPA: the machine never got a DHCP lease, so this is not a
# DNS problem. Check the link/switch port, then the DHCP scope:
Get-NetAdapter | Format-Table Name,Status
ipconfig /release; ipconfig /renew

exercises.prompt: A workstation can reach 10.20.0.10 on port 80 but cannot reach fileserver.ontrak.lab on port 80. Which layer is broken, and what is the fastest confirmation?
exercises.solution:
Resolve-DnsName fileserver.ontrak.lab -DnsOnly
Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4

objectives: Read the desktop network status and adapter list without a browser
Separate address, gateway, name-resolution and service failures
Collect the four commands of evidence a ticket needs

steps.body: The taskbar indicator and Settings > Network answer "is there a link and an address" in two clicks. It is not a substitute for the command line, but it tells you which branch to take, and a user can be talked through it on the phone.
steps.title: Start at the desktop

steps.body: If the adapter has an address in 169.254.x.x it never reached DHCP, and name resolution cannot be the fix yet. Fix the link, the DHCP scope or the switch port first. Only once there is a real address do DNS tests mean anything.
steps.title: Address before names

steps.body: Ping the default gateway by address. Success means routing works and the fault is further out; failure means the fault is here. Test the remote service by IP *and* by name: works by IP but not by name is, by definition, a name-resolution fault.
steps.title: Gateway, then the far side

steps.body: -DnsOnly forces a real DNS query. Without it, a hosts entry or a cached answer can make a broken resolver look healthy — which is exactly how "it works for me" tickets happen.
steps.title: Name resolution, tested honestly

steps.body: A ticket needs the client (hostname), the address it has, the resolver it is using, and the test result. Four lines. Whoever picks the ticket up next should not have to repeat your work.
steps.command: hostname; ipconfig | Select-String IPv4; Get-DnsClientServerAddress -AddressFamily IPv4
steps.title: Write the four lines down

win-network-diagnostics.yaml.summary: Work a "I have no network" ticket in the order that costs the least time: the desktop indicators first, then address, then name resolution, then the far end — in both the GUI and PowerShell, so the same evidence comes out either way.
win-network-diagnostics.yaml.title: Windows network diagnostics: from the desktop to the command line
